title: The pip package manager
game_role: Your package list appears in the game's credits.
objective: Learn what packages and pip are, and read and write requirements.txt files
story: Every day ships dock at the harbor of Discovery Island. Boxes from all over the world are unloaded: inside are ready-made tools built by other programmers. In the Python world these boxes are called **packages**, and the ship that brings them is called **pip**.

sections.title: What is a package?
sections.body:
A package is a collection of modules that someone wrote and shared with everyone. There are hundreds of thousands of Python packages, and they all live in a giant store called **PyPI** (the Python Package Index).

For example, `requests` makes getting data from the internet easy, `pygame` helps you make games, and `pandas` handles tables.

sections.title: pip commands
sections.body:
`pip` is the program that installs packages. These commands aren't written inside Python code; you type them in your computer's **terminal**:

```
pip install requests        # install
pip install pygame==2.5.2   # install a specific version
pip list                    # show installed packages
pip uninstall requests      # remove
pip freeze                  # list packages with their versions
```

sections.title: requirements.txt
sections.body:
The packages a project needs are written in a `requirements.txt` file. Each line has one package and its version:

```
requests==2.31.0
pygame==2.5.2
```

When someone else downloads your project, they install everything at once with `pip install -r requirements.txt`.

sections.title: Version numbers
sections.body:
Versions like `2.31.0` are read as **major.minor.patch**. Careful when comparing! If you compare them as text, `"2.4.1" > "2.31.0"` comes out True, because Python compares character by character and `4` is bigger than `3`. The right way is to turn the parts into numbers:

```python
v = tuple(int(p) for p in "2.31.0".split("."))   # (2, 31, 0)
```

A little surprise: run `import this`. That module comes with Python, so there's nothing to install.

examples.title: Split the line
examples.code:
line = "requests==2.31.0"
name, version = line.split("==")
print("Package:", name)
print("Version:", version)

examples.title: The version trap
examples.code:
a = "2.4.1"
b = "2.31.0"
print("As text:", a > b)
va = tuple(int(p) for p in a.split("."))
vb = tuple(int(p) for p in b.split("."))
print("As numbers:", va > vb)
examples.note: Which one is right? 31 is bigger than 4, so 2.31.0 is newer.

tasks.title: Split the line
tasks.prompt: Put the package name in `line` into `name` and the version into `version`.
tasks.solution:
line = "requests==2.31.0"

name, version = line.split("==")

print(name, version)
hints: line.split("==") gives a list with two parts.
You can spread them into two variables, like tuple unpacking.

tasks.title: Requirements reader
tasks.prompt: `text` holds the contents of a requirements.txt. Split each line and add it to the `packages` dictionary as `{package: version}`. Skip empty lines.
tasks.solution:
text = """requests==2.31.0
flask==3.0.0

numpy==1.26.4"""

packages = {}
for line in text.splitlines():
    line = line.strip()
    if line == "":
        continue
    name, version = line.split("==")
    packages[name] = version

print(packages)
hints: To skip an empty line: if line == "": continue

tasks.title: Which one is newer?
tasks.prompt: Compare the versions `v1` and `v2` **as numbers**. Store the newer one in `newer` (`v1` if they're equal).
tasks.starter:
v1 = "2.4.1"
v2 = "2.31.0"

newer = v1

print("Newer:", newer)
tasks.solution:
v1 = "2.4.1"
v2 = "2.31.0"

t1 = tuple(int(p) for p in v1.split("."))
t2 = tuple(int(p) for p in v2.split("."))
newer = v2 if t2 > t1 else v1

print("Newer:", newer)
hints: Turn the parts into ints and make a tuple; tuples compare like numbers.

challenge.title: Missing packages
challenge.prompt: `needed` holds the packages the project wants, `installed` the ones already installed. Put the packages that still need installing into `to_install`, in alphabetical order.
hints: Remember the set difference: needed - installed
sorted() gives the result as a list.

project_task.title: Package list
project_task.prompt:
Let's prepare a requirements.txt for people who want to run our game on their computer. From the `packages` dictionary, build the `requirements` text with one `name==version` line per package, in **alphabetical order**, and print it:

```
pygame==2.5.2
rich==13.7.0
```
project_task.solution:
packages = {"rich": "13.7.0", "pygame": "2.5.2"}

lines = [f"{name}=={version}" for name, version in sorted(packages.items())]
requirements = "\n".join(lines)

print(requirements)
hints: sorted(packages.items()) sorts the packages by name.
